name: Sci-Fi Predictions That Came True
description: Questions about real-world technologies and ideas often associated with science fiction.

questions.question: Robert A. Heinlein imagined portable “pocketphones” in his 1953 collection Assignment in Eternity. Which later device also lets people make calls while moving around?
questions.explanation_correct: Heinlein described portable phones before modern mobile phones became widespread. The resemblance alone does not establish that the stories caused their invention.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A paper encyclopedia, compass and slide rule are not portable telephone devices.

questions.question: In a 1945 Wireless World article, science-fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke proposed using stations in 24-hour Earth orbits for which purpose?
questions.explanation_correct: Clarke’s nonfiction article proposed orbiting stations to relay communications. Geostationary communications satellites were developed later; NASA notes others contributed to the field.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The article addressed communications satellites, not ocean research, mining or waste disposal.

questions.question: NASA history notes that reading Jules Verne helped inspire Robert H. Goddard to pursue which field?
questions.explanation_correct: Goddard pursued practical rocketry after reading Verne. Actual rockets developed through experimental science rather than the giant cannon in Verne’s lunar novel.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The NASA history discusses Goddard’s interest in space travel and rocketry, not the other fields.

questions.question: In a 1927 prediction, science-fiction publisher Hugo Gernsback described telephone conversations in which callers could also see each other. Which present-day service offers a comparable function?
questions.explanation_correct: Gernsback imagined distant callers seeing one another during a conversation. Modern video calls offer that feature, although the technology and services developed through many contributors.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Text messaging and radio broadcasting do not normally let both callers see each other live; printed newspapers are not a live conversation.

questions.question: According to the Smithsonian, the creator of Second Life credited which 1992 science-fiction novel with offering an inspiring picture of a virtual world?
questions.explanation_correct: Neal Stephenson’s Snow Crash depicts a virtual Metaverse; Second Life creator Philip Rosedale described its picture of a virtual world as inspiring.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other novels are different works; the cited creator specifically discussed Snow Crash.

questions.question: Frederik Pohl's 1966 novel The Age of the Pussyfoot imagined callers leaving recorded messages. What later phone feature offers a comparable function?
questions.explanation_correct: The novel described message-recording capabilities comparable to voicemail; this similarity does not establish that the novel caused its invention.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A compass provides direction, a flashlight provides light and a screen lock controls access, rather than recording messages from callers.

questions.question: According to the Smithsonian, Apple engineer Steve Perlman said an episode of Star Trek: The Next Generation helped inspire which multimedia software?
questions.explanation_correct: Perlman connected his idea for QuickTime with seeing a Star Trek character use a computer to play multiple music tracks.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Photoshop, Navigator and Excel are different products; the account names QuickTime.

questions.question: In Jules Verne’s From the Earth to the Moon, a giant cannon launches a crewed projectile. What launched the real Apollo Moon missions?
options: A magnetic rail on the Moon
questions.explanation_correct: Apollo crews launched on Saturn V rockets; Verne imagined a giant cannon, not a practicable crewed launcher.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Verne’s cannon was fictional; neither a balloon nor a lunar rail launched Apollo from Earth.

questions.question: Which aviation pioneer did the Smithsonian describe as inspired by Jules Verne’s Clipper of the Clouds as a child?
questions.explanation_correct: The Smithsonian identifies aviation pioneer Igor Sikorsky as having been inspired by Verne’s novel about a fictional flying machine.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Smithsonian account identifies Sikorsky; the other choices were aviators with different careers.

questions.question: Arthur C. Clarke's 'The Wind from the Sun' imagines a solar-sail race. Which real spacecraft demonstrated solar-sail propulsion in interplanetary space in 2010?
questions.explanation_correct: JAXA's IKAROS deployed a solar sail and demonstrated propulsion from sunlight in 2010. Clarke described a fictional race; the concept had earlier scientific roots.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Voyager 1, Apollo 11 and Viking 1 did not make this solar-sail demonstration.

questions.question: In H. G. Wells’s 1923 novel Men Like Gods, people send wireless messages that recipients collect later. Which modern service offers a comparable store-and-forward feature?
questions.explanation_correct: Email can store a message until its recipient accesses it. Wells’s fictional system is not evidence that the novel directly caused email to be invented.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Live radio is not the same store-and-forward service, and typewriters and compasses do not deliver electronic messages.

questions.question: NASA says which Star Wars device inspired the development of free-flying SPHERES robots tested aboard an orbital laboratory?
options: The training droid used by Luke Skywalker
questions.answer: The training droid used by Luke Skywalker
questions.explanation_correct: NASA describes the floating training droid from Star Wars as the inspiration for SPHERES, used for experiments including formation flight.
questions.explanation_incorrect: C-3PO is a humanoid protocol droid; the helmet and the Death Star are not the floating training robot.

questions.question: In Octavia Butler's 1993 novel Parable of the Sower, a community faces drought and fire. Which pair of real climate-related risks offers a limited parallel to those conditions?
options: Melting sea ice and coastal erosion
questions.explanation_correct: Butler imagined a future affected by drought and fire. Real climate risks include worsening heat and wildfire conditions in parts of California; the novel is not a literal forecast of every event.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ocean acidification, coastal flooding and sea-ice loss are distinct climate-related concerns rather than the heat-and-wildfire pair described here.

questions.question: In Back to the Future Part II, the future McFly home contains a wide, flat television on the wall. Which commonplace later device resembles that prop?
questions.explanation_correct: The 1989 film depicts a wall-mounted flat display, visually comparable to later flat-panel TVs. It did not predict every aspect of their design or adoption.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A tape recorder, typewriter and record player do not serve as the wall-mounted video display shown in the film.

questions.question: Robert Heinlein’s story Waldo features a remotely operated mechanical hand. What nickname was later used for real remote manipulator arms?
questions.explanation_correct: The Smithsonian reports that remote manipulator arms developed for the nuclear industry were called “waldos” after Heinlein’s fictional inventor.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Holodecks, tricorders and replicators are fictional Star Trek devices rather than that nickname.

questions.question: The Six Million Dollar Man imagined exceptional bionic abilities. Which real device can use electrical signals from remaining muscles to help move an artificial hand?
questions.explanation_correct: Some powered prosthetic hands use surface electrodes to detect muscle signals and control motors. They do not provide the fictional character's superhuman strength.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cochlear implants support hearing, insulin pumps deliver insulin, and pacemakers regulate heart rhythm; they do not control an artificial hand using muscle signals.

questions.question: H. G. Wells imagined recorded listening in When the Sleeper Wakes. Which modern format similarly lets a person listen to a narrated book?
questions.explanation_correct: The Smithsonian describes audiobook-like entertainment in Wells’s novel; a modern audiobook is a recorded narration of a book.
questions.explanation_incorrect: An atlas and a paper newspaper are printed formats; a silent film is primarily visual.

questions.question: In Arthur C. Clarke’s Rendezvous with Rama, Spaceguard monitors possible impacts from space. What do real near-Earth-object surveys track for a comparable purpose?
questions.explanation_correct: NASA tracks near-Earth objects, including asteroids and comets, to assess possible impacts; Spaceguard was Clarke’s fictional organization.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other choices are not near-Earth objects monitored for an impact from space.

questions.question: In the film 2001: A Space Odyssey, a large rotating space station appears in Earth orbit. Which real structure has hosted crews in orbit since 2000?
questions.explanation_correct: The ISS is an inhabited orbital laboratory. Unlike the fictional rotating wheel, it does not provide artificial gravity through rotation.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other structures are on or under Earth and are not inhabited orbital laboratories.

questions.question: Captain Nemo's Nautilus in Jules Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea is what kind of vessel?
questions.explanation_correct: Nemo's Nautilus is a fictional submarine. Real submersibles existed before Verne's novel, while later submarines developed different capabilities and power sources.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Airships fly, space stations orbit Earth, and hovercraft ride on an air cushion; none describes the Nautilus.

questions.question: Which 1996 Motorola flip phone took its name in part from the Star Trek series and resembled its fictional communicator?
questions.explanation_correct: The Smithsonian connects the StarTAC flip phone with Star Trek’s 1966 communicator; the devices are not identical.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The iPhone 4, Nokia 3310 and BlackBerry 850 were other mobile devices, not the StarTAC.

questions.question: H. G. Wells's nonfiction idea of a 'World Brain' imagined widely accessible knowledge. Which modern collaborative project offers a limited comparison?
questions.explanation_correct: Wells envisioned a shared repository of knowledge. Wikipedia is a collaboratively edited online encyclopedia; it is not an implementation of a detailed Wells design.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other options are not collaborative online reference projects.

questions.question: Karel Čapek’s play R.U.R. helped introduce which word for artificial workers into common use?
questions.explanation_correct: R.U.R. introduced the word “robot” in the context of artificial workers. Čapek’s fictional beings are not the same as modern industrial machines.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Satellites, telescopes and algorithms are different concepts and are not the term introduced by the play.

questions.question: A 1994 NASA contractor report compared which room-sized visualization system to Star Trek's fictional holodeck?
questions.explanation_correct: The report described CAVE as a large environment in which a user could view and interact with virtual visualizations. It did not have the holodeck’s fictional capabilities.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other choices are navigation or communications systems and a space telescope, not the cited immersive room.

questions.question: Andy Weir's Project Hail Mary imagines a deep-space mission. What real NASA network uses large radio antennas to communicate with distant spacecraft?
options: Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System
questions.explanation_correct: NASA uses the Deep Space Network to send and receive radio messages to distant spacecraft. This is a limited real-world comparison, not the fictional mission itself.
questions.explanation_incorrect: GPS supports navigation; NASA’s relay satellites support communications with spacecraft near Earth, while the Deep Space Network is used for distant missions.

questions.question: Arthur C. Clarke’s The Fountains of Paradise imagines a space elevator. In a NASA-funded challenge addressing a related engineering problem, what did LaserMotive’s robot climb in 2009?
options: A ladder attached to the International Space Station
A cable connecting Earth to an orbiting station
A one-kilometre cable suspended from a helicopter
A mountain railway on the Moon
questions.answer: A one-kilometre cable suspended from a helicopter
questions.explanation_correct: The laser-powered robot climbed a one-kilometre cable during the challenge. This demonstrated a component-related concept, not a working elevator to orbit.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The test used a cable suspended from a helicopter, not a structure reaching orbit or the Moon.

questions.question: According to the Smithsonian, which submarine designer was inspired as a child by Jules Verne’s Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea?
questions.explanation_correct: The Smithsonian recounts that Simon Lake read Verne as a child and later designed submarines; Verne did not invent the submarine.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sikorsky worked on helicopters, Goddard on rockets, and Clarke was a science-fiction writer.

questions.question: In 2001: A Space Odyssey, what is the name of the talking computer that helps control Discovery One?
questions.explanation_correct: HAL 9000 is a fictional ship computer. Modern speech interfaces have limited capabilities and do not reproduce HAL’s fictional general intelligence.
questions.explanation_incorrect: R2-D2 and the T-800 are characters from other franchises; the Iron Giant is a different fictional robot.

questions.question: George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four portrays pervasive state surveillance. Which real technology can record video in a monitored public space, providing a limited comparison?
questions.explanation_correct: Closed-circuit cameras can transmit footage for monitoring. The specific use, reach and laws governing real surveillance vary; a camera alone is not Orwell's whole surveillance state.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A fingerprint reader identifies biometric patterns, a card reader controls access, and a microphone records sound; none is a video camera.

questions.question: Which modern device is a limited real-world analogue of the voice-operated ship computer in Star Trek?
questions.explanation_correct: A smart speaker can respond to spoken commands through a virtual assistant. It resembles one function of the fictional computer, not its full intelligence or capabilities.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A thermostat, Wi-Fi router and smart hub have other primary functions, though some smart hubs also offer voice control.

questions.question: In a 1925 Science and Invention article, Hugo Gernsback imagined the Teledactyl. Which modern practice similarly allows a doctor and patient to talk by video from different locations?
questions.explanation_correct: Video visits allow remote communication. Gernsback also imagined remotely controlled arms with touch feedback; ordinary video visits do not reproduce that device.
questions.explanation_incorrect: MRI produces images, genetic sequencing reads DNA, and 3D printing makes objects; none means a remote video consultation.

questions.question: NASA compared Ray Bradbury's fictional solar-sampling story The Golden Apples of the Sun with its Genesis mission. What did Genesis actually collect for study?
options: A solid piece of the Sun
questions.explanation_correct: Genesis collected solar-wind particles and returned samples to Earth. Bradbury’s fictional crew scoops up material from the Sun; the real mission did not touch the solar surface.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Genesis collected particles streaming from the Sun, not a solid fragment, core material, or lunar rocks.

questions.question: In Star Trek: The Next Generation, Geordi La Forge wears a VISOR that helps him perceive his surroundings. NASA compared it with JORDY, a real device designed to assist people with what condition?
questions.explanation_correct: NASA describes JORDY as a wearable optical device intended to help people with low vision with activities such as reading and watching television. It is not equivalent to Geordi’s fictional VISOR.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hearing, balance and smell are different senses; JORDY was designed as a visual aid.

questions.question: Which modern portable device resembles the flat, hand-held information displays used aboard Star Trek spacecraft?
questions.explanation_correct: Tablet computers resemble the portable displays shown in Star Trek. The resemblance concerns the form and some functions; it does not establish that every tablet was inspired by the show.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Notebook PCs generally have attached keyboards; handheld consoles and smart displays have different primary designs.

questions.question: In a 1964 essay about life in 2014, science-fiction writer Isaac Asimov envisioned cars with automated features. What modern technology offers a limited comparison?
questions.explanation_correct: Automated driving systems can assist or perform parts of driving in defined conditions. Their capabilities and need for supervision vary; they do not make Asimov’s imagined future a literal match.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Parking meters, paper maps and manual wipers do not themselves automate the driving task.

questions.question: Which real communication technology resembles the video calls shown in the 1960s cartoon The Jetsons?
questions.explanation_correct: Video calls transmit moving images and sound between people, as did the show’s fictional videophones.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Text messages, voice-only calls and podcasts do not provide the same live two-way video conversation.

questions.question: Star Trek’s fictional universal translator lets people communicate across languages. Which real software system translated technical documents for the Apollo–Soyuz mission?
questions.explanation_correct: NASA reports that SYSTRAN translated technical documents exchanged for Apollo–Soyuz. It did not match the fictional device’s instantaneous, universal speech translation.
questions.explanation_incorrect: ELIZA was an early conversational program; FORTRAN and COBOL are programming languages rather than the translation system named here.

questions.question: Dick Tracy used a two-way wrist radio in the comic strip from 1946. Which modern device can similarly support wrist-worn voice communication?
questions.explanation_correct: Some smartwatches support voice calls, echoing the wrist-worn radio used by Dick Tracy. A modern smartwatch also performs many other functions.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A pedometer counts steps, a fitness band mainly tracks activity, and a chronometer measures time; none necessarily supports voice calls.

questions.question: Edward Bellamy’s Looking Backward describes a future payment item. Which present-day cashless payment tool shares that general function?
questions.explanation_correct: Bellamy used the term in an imagined economic system. Modern credit cards work within different banking arrangements, so the similarity is not proof of direct invention.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Maps, film tickets and shelves are not the payment cards named in the question.

questions.question: How did the fictional crew in Jules Verne’s Around the Moon travel relative to the Moon, before real astronauts orbited it?
options: They built a permanent lunar base
They landed and walked on the Moon
They drove across the Moon in a rover
questions.explanation_correct: NASA’s history notes that Verne’s sequel depicted a journey around the Moon without a lunar landing; Apollo 8 later carried humans around it.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Verne’s travelers did not land, drive on the surface or build a lunar base in that story.

questions.question: Which destructive technology did H.G. Wells describe in 'The World Set Free' long before its development?
questions.explanation_correct: H. G. Wells described “atomic bombs” in his 1914 novel The World Set Free, decades before nuclear weapons were built; his fictional mechanism differed from real bombs.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other options refer to specific variants or radiological devices that were categorized later in historical military development.

questions.question: Which real technology can immerse a user in a computer-generated environment, a limited analogue of the holodeck in Star Trek?
questions.explanation_correct: Virtual reality can immerse users in simulated environments, often using a headset. Current systems do not recreate the holodeck’s fully physical simulated world.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Augmented and mixed reality combine digital content with physical surroundings; extended reality is an umbrella term that includes VR.

questions.question: Star Trek depicts a transporter moving people. What do real quantum-teleportation experiments transfer between distant systems?
options: A physical object in its entirety
questions.explanation_correct: Quantum teleportation transfers an unknown quantum state using entanglement and classical communication. It does not transport a person or send usable information faster than light.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Real quantum-teleportation experiments do not move an entire person, spacecraft or object as a fictional transporter does.

questions.question: What term, popularized in William Gibson's Neuromancer, was used to describe a consensual hallucination experienced as a global network?
questions.explanation_correct: Gibson coined “cyberspace” in the 1982 story Burning Chrome and popularized it in the 1984 novel Neuromancer.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other terms represent specific network layers or modern conceptual iterations rather than the original literary construct.

questions.question: NASA engineer Les Johnson recalled that The Mote in God's Eye sparked his interest in which propulsion concept?
questions.explanation_correct: Johnson said that the spacecraft sails in the Niven and Pournelle novel stayed with him before he later worked on solar-sail technology at NASA.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Johnson described large sails driven by sunlight and lasers, not the other propulsion concepts listed.

questions.question: Isaac Asimov’s story “Reason” describes a solar power station in space. What existing technology can convert sunlight directly into electricity aboard spacecraft?
questions.explanation_correct: Asimov later discussed the fictional station as an idea for space-based solar power. Real photovoltaic cells convert sunlight into electricity, including on spacecraft; they do not establish the large power network described in fiction.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rocket engines provide propulsion, radar altimeters measure distance, and compasses indicate direction; none is a photovoltaic power source.

questions.question: The name of which real electrical device was inspired by a fictional invention associated with the young science-fiction hero Tom Swift?
questions.explanation_correct: The Smithsonian reports that inventor Jack Cover named TASER after a fictional electric rifle associated with Tom Swift. The fictional rifle and the real device are not identical.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Geiger counters measure ionizing radiation; AEDs and pacemakers have medical purposes and are not the device named in the source.

questions.question: NASA has compared which real process for building objects from digital designs with the fictional Star Trek replicator?
questions.explanation_correct: 3D printing creates objects by adding material in layers. NASA has drawn a comparison with Star Trek replicators, which are depicted as far more versatile.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Milling and carving remove material, while casting uses a mold; none is the additive process described.

questions.question: In H. G. Wells’s The War of the Worlds, what fictional weapon do the Martians use to burn targets from a distance?
questions.explanation_correct: Wells imagined a heat-ray decades before the first working laser. A fictional heat-ray is not technically identical to every real laser.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other devices are different fictional concepts and are not the Martians’ heat-ray.

questions.question: NASA engineer Marc Rayman said he first heard of ion propulsion in a Star Trek episode. Which NASA spacecraft later tested an ion engine in interplanetary space?
questions.explanation_correct: Deep Space 1, launched in 1998, tested ion propulsion. Rayman linked his first encounter with the concept to Star Trek; this does not mean the series invented ion propulsion.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Apollo 11, Pioneer 10 and Vostok 1 were different missions and were not NASA’s Deep Space 1 ion-propulsion test spacecraft.

questions.question: NASA compares Voyager’s autonomous fault-protection programming with HAL from 2001: A Space Odyssey. What does the real programming help Voyager do?
options: Detect and respond to spacecraft faults
Control a rotating fictional space station
questions.answer: Detect and respond to spacecraft faults
questions.explanation_correct: NASA notes that both Voyager spacecraft have programming for autonomous fault protection. This limited function is not equivalent to HAL’s fictional intelligence.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other options describe fictional or unrelated capabilities rather than Voyager’s fault-protection programming.

questions.question: According to a 1947 letter described by Smithsonian, a command ship in E. E. “Doc” Smith’s Lensmen novels inspired a naval officer to introduce what shipboard facility?
questions.explanation_correct: Smithsonian recounts a 1947 letter attributing the introduction of combat information centers to an officer inspired by Smith’s fictional command ship. This is an attributed historical account.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A galley prepares food, a dry dock supports vessel maintenance, and a magazine stores ammunition.

questions.question: Which NASA shuttle test vehicle was named after the Star Trek starship following a fan letter-writing campaign?
questions.explanation_correct: NASA named its atmospheric test orbiter Enterprise after a campaign by Star Trek fans; it was not built to fly in space.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Columbia, Challenger and Discovery were other shuttle orbiters; the Star Trek namesake was Enterprise.

questions.question: Aldous Huxley’s 1932 novel Brave New World depicts human fertilization outside the body. Which later medical technique also involves fertilization outside the body?
questions.explanation_correct: IVF involves fertilizing an egg in a laboratory and, when appropriate, transferring an embryo to the uterus. Huxley imagined artificial reproduction and gestation on a much larger scale; real IVF is not the novel’s system.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Dialysis, radiotherapy and ultrasound imaging do not fertilize an egg.

questions.question: In a 1959 essay, science-fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke described a pocket-sized personal transceiver. Besides making calls, what could his imagined device determine?
options: The chemical composition of distant planets
The age of the surrounding rocks
questions.explanation_correct: NASA’s history notes that Clarke predicted a small personal communicator able to determine a person’s position. Smartphones with satellite navigation offer a limited parallel; the essay was nonfiction.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Clarke described a communicator that could determine its user’s position, rather than analyse blood, planets or rocks.

questions.question: The 1896 serial In the Deep of Time by George Parsons Lathrop, developed from Thomas Edison’s notes, depicts uncrewed flying machines delivering mail. What later service uses a broadly similar idea?
questions.explanation_correct: In the Deep of Time depicts uncrewed airborne mail delivery. The FAA describes commercial drones delivering packages and medical supplies; this resemblance does not establish a causal link.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other options do not describe packages carried through the air by an uncrewed aircraft.

questions.question: According to Smithsonian, which physicist was inspired by H. G. Wells’s The World Set Free while thinking about a nuclear chain reaction?
questions.explanation_correct: Smithsonian reports that Szilard read Wells’s novel and was inspired to consider a nuclear chain reaction. This describes an influence on one scientist, not a claim that the novel alone created nuclear technology.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Smithsonian identifies Szilard, who read the novel before his 1933 chain-reaction idea.

questions.question: In the 1896 serial In the Deep of Time by George Parsons Lathrop, developed from Thomas Edison’s notes, electric vehicles can recharge at hotels. Which modern infrastructure serves a similar purpose for electric cars?
questions.explanation_correct: The fictional vehicles could recharge away from home. Modern electric-vehicle charging stations also supply electricity to vehicle batteries, though electric vehicles existed before the story and its resemblance does not establish an influence.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Petrol pumps supply fuel, while railway turntables and dry docks serve different transport needs.

questions.question: The film Minority Report shows a computer interface controlled by hand movements. What similar input method does the real g-speak system use?
questions.explanation_correct: MIT reports that John Underkoffler designed the film interface and later developed g-speak. His gesture-interface research had already begun before the film; the real system does not reproduce every fictional capability.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Both the fictional interface and g-speak use hand gestures, rather than paper forms, rotary dials or punched cards.

questions.question: Which real household device performs one cleaning task, offering a limited comparison with Rosie, the robot housekeeper in The Jetsons?
questions.explanation_correct: The Smithsonian compares Rosie with robotic vacuums while noting that real vacuums perform far fewer tasks than the fictional housekeeper.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rice cookers, thermostats and flashlights are not autonomous floor-cleaning robots.

questions.question: In a 1951 proposal, science-fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke described satellites observing Earth as it rotated. Which civilian Earth-observation program launched its first satellite in 1972?
questions.explanation_correct: NASA notes that Clarke proposed observations from polar-orbiting satellites in 1951; the first Landsat spacecraft began Earth observations in 1972. The comparison does not establish that Clarke invented the program.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Voyager explores the outer solar system, while Apollo and Artemis are human spaceflight programs rather than the Earth-observation program named here.

questions.question: Ray Bradbury’s story “There Will Come Soft Rains” depicts a house that carries out routines automatically. Which modern device offers a limited example of home automation?
questions.explanation_correct: A programmable thermostat can change a home’s heating or cooling settings on a schedule. Unlike Bradbury’s fictional house, it performs only a limited function.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A manual switch, doorstop and handbell do not by themselves carry out a scheduled home-control routine.

questions.question: What does Neal Stephenson call the shared computer-generated world visited through avatars in his 1992 novel Snow Crash?
options: The Oasis of Ready Player One
questions.explanation_correct: Snow Crash presents the Metaverse as a shared computer-generated environment whose users appear as avatars; real social virtual worlds resemble parts of the idea.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other choices refer to different fictional settings, not the virtual world named in Snow Crash.

questions.question: The Martian imagines astronauts working on Mars. What is NASA’s HERA, used to study aspects of a mission without traveling to Mars?
options: A crewed base on the surface of Mars
A spacecraft that has carried people to Mars
A simulated mission habitat on Earth
questions.answer: A simulated mission habitat on Earth
questions.explanation_correct: HERA is a ground-based analog where crews live and work during simulated missions, including studies of confinement and communication delays.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other options describe missions or installations that HERA is not; HERA remains on Earth.

questions.question: Researcher Ariel Ekblaw has cited Neal Stephenson’s Seveneves as inspiration for small crawling robots. What can the real MIT Rovables prototypes do?
options: Repair human organs from inside the body
Build a space station without human assistance
questions.explanation_correct: Ekblaw described Rovables as small robots that crawl on clothing using magnetic wheels. Their limited capabilities are distinct from the robots imagined in the novel.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rovables are miniature robots that move on clothing; the other choices describe different or fictional capabilities.

questions.question: In The Martian, Mark Watney grows potatoes. Which leafy crop was actually grown and eaten by astronauts using NASA’s Veggie system on the ISS?
questions.explanation_correct: NASA astronauts ate red romaine lettuce grown in the Veggie system aboard the ISS. NASA researchers caution that the film’s use of untreated Martian material is not a working recipe.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Bananas, wild Martian mushrooms and ocean kelp were not the Veggie lettuce crop described.

questions.question: In Primo Levi’s 1964 story Order on the Cheap, a machine copies objects in thin layers. Which modern process also builds objects layer by layer?
questions.explanation_correct: Levi’s fictional Mimer copies an object in thin layers. Many 3D printers build objects layer by layer from a digital design; that resemblance does not mean current printers can duplicate anything the fictional machine can.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Paper photocopying, radio broadcasting and distillation do not build three-dimensional objects layer by layer.

questions.question: In William Gibson’s Neuromancer, characters connect to cyberspace through neural implants. What real research field studies interfaces between neural signals and external devices?
questions.explanation_correct: Brain-computer interfaces can connect neural signals to external devices in limited ways; they do not recreate Gibson’s full immersive fictional network.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Solar cells, maglev and fiber-optic cables are not interfaces that directly use neural activity.

questions.question: In Arthur C. Clarke’s novel 2001: A Space Odyssey, a monolith is found on Saturn’s moon Iapetus. Which real spacecraft flew close to Iapetus in 2007?
questions.explanation_correct: NASA’s Cassini spacecraft flew by Iapetus in 2007. Unlike Clarke’s fictional crewed journey and monolith, Cassini was an uncrewed scientific spacecraft.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cassini made the 2007 flyby of Saturn’s moon; Juno, New Horizons and Parker Solar Probe were different missions.

questions.question: In Star Wars, R2-D2 projects an apparently free-standing image of Leia. Which real optical technology can record interference patterns to create a three-dimensional appearance?
questions.explanation_correct: Holography records an interference pattern that can reconstruct a three-dimensional appearance. Existing holograms do not behave like Leia’s free-standing projected image.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sonar and ultrasound use sound; radio broadcasting transmits signals and does not itself describe holographic image recording.

questions.question: In the film Minority Report, signs identify passersby and address them with personalized ads. Which real practice also tailors some ads, although it need not use an eye scan?
options: Broadcasting the same radio signal to all listeners
Showing every visitor the same static banner
Targeting online ads using browsing history
questions.answer: Targeting online ads using browsing history
questions.explanation_correct: The FTC describes online advertising based on browsing history or location. That practice is a limited comparison with the film’s fictional iris-scanning billboards, not the same system.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Identical posters, a shared radio broadcast and a static banner do not describe tailoring an ad to browsing history.

questions.question: David H. Keller’s 1933 story Unto Us a Child Is Born imagines a compact automatic food-making machine. Which real appliance is a limited comparison because it heats meals from prepared ingredient pods?
questions.explanation_correct: Keller’s fictional appliance makes and prepares food automatically. The Genie prepares meals from pods of prepared ingredients, so the real device is a limited comparison to the fictional machine.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other devices are not appliances for preparing food.

questions.question: In Ray Bradbury’s Fahrenheit 451, tiny “Seashell” radios are worn in the ear. Which later personal audio device is a partial real-world analogue?
questions.explanation_correct: Bradbury imagined small in-ear radios; wireless earbuds similarly place audio devices in the ear, though their functions and technologies differ.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A television, printer and typewriter are not personal in-ear audio devices.

questions.question: In Arthur C. Clarke’s 2010: Odyssey Two, Europa is home to fictional life. Which real NASA spacecraft investigated Jupiter and provided evidence of a possible ocean beneath Europa’s ice?
questions.explanation_correct: Galileo investigated Jupiter and its moons. Its measurements supported the case for a subsurface ocean on Europa, but no life has been confirmed there; the fictional life is not a prediction proven true.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The question concerns Galileo’s observations of Europa, not a Mars rover, a record carried on Voyager or Hubble.

questions.question: Which Star Trek instrument does NASA compare with its real handheld STELLA environmental sensor?
questions.explanation_correct: STELLA records environmental measurements such as light and temperature. It is a limited educational tool, not a complete fictional tricorder.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A transporter moves people in fiction, a warp drive propels a fictional ship and a photon torpedo is a fictional weapon.

questions.question: H. G. Wells's 1903 story 'The Land Ironclads' describes armoured fighting vehicles crossing trenches. Which later military vehicle shares that broad role?
questions.explanation_correct: Wells imagined huge armoured vehicles crossing trenches before tanks appeared on the battlefield. His machines used pedrail wheels, not the tracks of typical tanks.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other vehicles are not armoured battlefield vehicles designed to cross trenches.

questions.question: Star Wars shows droids assisting people in space. What NASA humanoid robot was tested aboard the ISS?
questions.explanation_correct: Robonaut 2 was a humanoid research robot tested on the ISS. It is not an autonomous personality like a fictional Star Wars droid.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Voyager 1 is a probe, while Kepler and Hubble are space observatories rather than humanoid ISS robots.

questions.question: Isaac Asimov's story 'Robbie' imagined a robot assisting a person. Which real programmable machine is designed to pick up and move objects between stations on a factory line?
questions.explanation_correct: An industrial robotic arm can perform programmed manipulation on a factory line. Its specialized tasks differ from those of Asimov's fictional domestic robot Robbie.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Barcode scanners read codes; 3D printers add material, and CNC milling machines remove material, rather than serving primarily to transfer objects between stations.

questions.question: Albert Robida's 1883 novel 'Le Vingtième Siècle' imagined news reaching homes through a telephonoscope. Which later medium similarly shows news on a screen?
questions.explanation_correct: Robida imagined a screen transmitting sound and pictures, including news, a parallel to television. This similarity does not establish that his work invented television.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Newspapers, records and paper maps do not show audiovisual news on a screen.

questions.question: Smithsonian compared an automated banking device in Ray Bradbury's Fahrenheit 451 with which later common banking machine?
questions.explanation_correct: Smithsonian noted a similarity between an automated banking station in the novel and an ATM; a comparison does not establish a direct line of invention.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Film projectors, photocopiers and traffic signals serve functions other than automated banking.

questions.question: Jules Verne's 'Around the Moon' depicts travellers going around the Moon. Which NASA mission later carried humans into lunar orbit for the first time?
questions.explanation_correct: Apollo 8 entered lunar orbit in 1968, nearly a century after Verne's imagined voyage. The novel's cannon launch was very different from NASA's rocket.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Apollo 11 made the first crewed lunar landing; Gemini 4 and Mercury-Atlas 6 stayed in Earth orbit.

questions.question: NASA compared Kepler-16 b with Tatooine from Star Wars because the real planet shares which feature of the fictional setting?
options: It has a confirmed desert surface
It has an artificial city covering its surface
questions.explanation_correct: Kepler-16 b orbits two stars, a limited parallel to Tatooine’s double sunset. NASA describes the real planet as a gas giant, not a confirmed desert world.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Its orbit is the point of comparison; a desert surface, human inhabitants and a planet-wide city have not been established for Kepler-16 b.

questions.question: Michael Crichton's 'The Andromeda Strain' imagines danger from an extraterrestrial organism. What precaution did NASA take with the first crews returning from the Moon?
options: They were sent back into orbit
questions.explanation_correct: NASA quarantined the first three crews returning from the lunar surface as a precaution against possible contamination. The story's dangerous organism was fictional.
questions.explanation_incorrect: NASA quarantined those astronauts on Earth; it did not send them back into orbit or keep them underwater.

questions.question: Star Trek's replicator can produce meals. According to Smithsonian, what does the real Genie appliance use to prepare food?
questions.explanation_correct: Smithsonian describes Genie as a Star Trek-inspired appliance that uses pods of dehydrated ingredients. It does not create food from energy as the fictional replicator does.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Genie uses prepared food ingredients, rather than assembling a meal from raw atoms, moon dust or sunlight.

questions.question: The robotic spacecraft Jules Verne, named for the science-fiction author, docked with the ISS in 2008. What was it designed to deliver?
options: A crew for a Moon landing
questions.explanation_correct: ESA's Automated Transfer Vehicle Jules Verne was an uncrewed cargo spacecraft for the ISS. Its name honoured the author; it was not the spacecraft from his novels.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The vehicle carried cargo to the ISS, not a lunar crew, a Mars rover or a replacement Moon.

questions.question: In Jules Verne's 'Around the Moon', the travellers return to Earth in a projectile that lands in the ocean. Where did NASA's Apollo 11 command module land on its return?
questions.explanation_correct: Both Verne's fictional projectile and Apollo 11's command module returned to the Pacific. Unlike the fictional projectile, Apollo 11 used parachutes to slow its descent.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Apollo 11 splashed down in the Pacific, where its crew and command module were recovered.

questions.question: Jules Verne imagined Captain Nemo’s submarine Nautilus. What powered the real USS Nautilus (SSN-571), which reached the North Pole under the ice in 1958?
questions.explanation_correct: USS Nautilus was the first nuclear-powered submarine and reached the North Pole beneath the ice in 1958. It shared a name with Verne’s fictional vessel but used a real nuclear propulsion plant.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sails and wind turbines use wind, while solar panels need light; the USS Nautilus used nuclear propulsion.

questions.question: In Isaac Asimov’s 1977 story “True Love,” a computer searches personal data to select a compatible partner for Milton. Which modern service offers a limited parallel through profiles and match recommendations?
questions.explanation_correct: Some dating services recommend profiles using information users provide and their activity. Their methods and data are limited; Asimov’s fictional computer has far broader access. The resemblance does not show that the story caused the service.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Messaging, virtual reality and general social networks can connect people, but dating services specifically present potential romantic matches.

questions.question: In E. M. Forster’s 1909 story The Machine Stops, Vashti gives a lecture while she and her audience remain in separate rooms. Which modern activity offers a similar form of remote teaching?
questions.explanation_correct: Forster describes an audience seeing and hearing a speaker remotely. Live online lectures enable a comparable interaction, although their technology and social setting differ from the story.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The fictional audience remotely sees and hears the lecturer, resembling a live online lecture rather than the other activities.

questions.question: Alexander Belyaev’s science-fiction story “Professor Dowell’s Head” imagines a head sustained by artificial circulation. Which real technology keeps a donor heart warm while perfusing it with oxygen and nutrients before transplantation?
questions.explanation_correct: An FDA-approved Organ Care System keeps the donor heart warm and supplies oxygen and nutrients by perfusing it before transplantation. This is a limited comparison with Belyaev’s fictional life-support apparatus; it does not preserve a detached head.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Dialysis filters blood and bypass surgery reroutes blood flow in a patient. Cold static storage preserves an organ without keeping it warm and perfusing it with oxygen and nutrients.

questions.question: NASA compared its experimental X1 robotic exoskeleton with the powered armor of which fictional superhero?
questions.explanation_correct: NASA used Iron Man as a comparison while explaining that X1 could assist or resist leg movement and lacked the abilities of the fictional armor.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The cited NASA comparison names Iron Man, not the other listed superheroes.

questions.question: Star Trek characters speak requests to the Enterprise computer. Which voice assistant did Apple introduce with the iPhone 4S in 2011, offering a limited real-world parallel?
questions.explanation_correct: Siri accepts spoken requests for everyday tasks, but it is far more limited than the fictional Enterprise computer.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Siri is Apple’s voice assistant; Alexa, Cortana and Google Assistant are associated with other companies. The comparison does not establish that Star Trek inspired Siri.

questions.question: The X-wing targeting computer in Star Wars: A New Hope has a limited visual parallel in aircraft displays. What is the name of the system that presents flight information on a transparent screen in the pilot’s forward view?
questions.explanation_correct: A real aircraft heads-up display projects flight information on a transparent screen in the pilot’s forward field of view. This is a limited display analogy, not a claim that the fictional targeting computer has the same function or that the film caused HUD development.
questions.explanation_incorrect: An LCD is a display-panel technology, a virtual desktop is a computing environment, and a speaker produces sound; none names this forward-view flight display.

questions.question: In Murray Leinster’s 1946 story “A Logic Named Joe,” household terminals connect through a network of information systems. Which later underlying network is the closest broad analogy to the system connecting them?
questions.explanation_correct: The Internet is a network of networks connecting computers. The World Wide Web is a hypertext information system that runs over it, and Usenet is a distributed discussion system that uses it; the Deep Web is web content not indexed by standard search engines. The story is only a broad analogy, not a technical design for today's Internet.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Web and Usenet use the Internet, while the Deep Web refers to web content outside standard search indexes; none is the underlying network connecting computers. The resemblance does not show that the story caused these systems.

questions.question: NASA compared its Chemical Laptop with Star Trek’s tricorder. What must the real instrument do to analyze material?
options: Take a sample into the instrument
Transport a person across a room
questions.answer: Take a sample into the instrument
questions.explanation_correct: NASA describes the Chemical Laptop as a compact sample analyzer and notes that, unlike the fictional tricorder, it must ingest a sample.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Instant universal diagnosis, transporting people and creating food exceed the specific real device described by NASA.

questions.question: Margaret Atwood’s Oryx and Crake imagines genetically engineered animals called pigoons. Which real research field applies engineering principles to design or redesign biological systems for useful purposes?
questions.explanation_correct: NIST describes synthetic biology, also called engineering biology, as intentionally designing and deploying living cells, cell systems and biological processes. That broad field is only a limited analogue to Atwood’s fictional pigoons; it does not make the novel’s organisms real.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Genetic counseling supports people making decisions about genetic conditions; evolutionary biology studies evolutionary processes, and molecular physiology examines how biological functions work.

questions.question: NASA compared its MOXIE Mars experiment with resource-use ideas in The Martian. What did MOXIE produce from Martian carbon dioxide?
questions.explanation_correct: MOXIE demonstrated oxygen production from carbon dioxide in the Martian atmosphere. It was an experiment, not the complete life-support system imagined for future crews.
questions.explanation_incorrect: MOXIE did not directly produce drinking water, methane or potatoes.

questions.question: NASA used its Mars Trek mapping tool to trace the journey of which fictional astronaut from Andy Weir’s novel The Martian across real Martian terrain?
questions.explanation_correct: NASA’s Mars Trek release explicitly lets users follow Mark Watney’s route from The Martian over mapped Martian terrain. It is an educational web map tied to the novel, not a claim that the fictional journey happened.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Dave Bowman is from 2001: A Space Odyssey, Klaatu is from The Day the Earth Stood Still, and John Carter is from Barsoom fiction.

questions.question: In The Martian, Mark Watney must conserve water to survive. Which real technology used aboard the ISS addresses a related resource challenge?
options: An underground Martian lake in the station
A device that creates unlimited water from nothing
questions.explanation_correct: NASA uses water-recovery systems aboard the ISS as part of life support. This is a limited comparison with the fictional challenge of conserving water on Mars; the circumstances and systems are different.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The ISS does not use a Martian lake or a faster-than-light delivery system, and water recovery does not create unlimited water from nothing.

questions.question: The Star Trek replicator creates objects on demand. What kind of items was the real eForge 3D printer designed to produce using NASA-funded research?
questions.explanation_correct: NASA reports that Electronic Alchemy’s eForge was designed to print electronic devices, drawing on research into making items on demand. It does not reproduce the fictional replicator’s broad capabilities.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The real printer was developed for electronics; the other choices exceed the specific capability described by NASA.
